reason: The sources provide multi-site corroboration for more than a dozen detailed facts about Apollo 12 and the TV camera incident.
story: In November 1969, Apollo 12 touched down on the Moon's Ocean of Storms, carrying the first color television camera ever brought to the lunar surface. Four months after Apollo 11's grainy black-and-white broadcast, viewers on Earth were eager to see the Moon in vivid color. But less than an hour into the first moonwalk, astronaut Alan Bean unclipped the Westinghouse camera to mount it on a tripod. Moving in his bulky suit, Bean accidentally pointed the camera lens directly into the blazing Sun. The intense solar radiation instantly scorched the camera's delicate light-sensitive tube. Seeing the broadcast drop out, Bean attempted the ultimate low-tech repair—whacking the top of the space-age camera with his geology hammer. It stayed broken, abruptly killing the live broadcast for millions of viewers. For the rest of the mission, visual records were limited to still film and Bean's vivid memories.
angle: When NASA sent the first color TV camera to the lunar surface, an astronaut ruined it within minutes by pointing it directly at the Sun—and tried fixing it by hitting it with a hammer.

claims.claim: Apollo 12 was the second crewed mission to land on the Moon, touching down on November 19, 1969.
Astronauts Charles Pete Conrad and Alan Bean landed on the Moon in the lunar module Intrepid.
Command Module Pilot Richard Gordon remained in lunar orbit while Conrad and Bean descended to the surface.
The landing took place in the lunar region known as the Ocean of Storms.
Apollo 12 made a precision landing within walking distance of the robotic Surveyor 3 spacecraft, which arrived in 1967.
Apollo 12 brought the first color television camera taken by an Apollo mission to the lunar surface, upgrading from Apollo 11's black-and-white camera.
The color TV camera utilized a sensitive secondary electron conduction (SEC) tube and a spinning color filter wheel.
While moving the camera to set it on a tripod, Alan Bean accidentally pointed its lens directly at the Sun.
Direct sunlight burned out the target of the camera's image tube, damaging it beyond repair.
Suspecting a stuck color wheel or internal fault, Bean hit the top of the camera with his hammer in an unsuccessful attempt to restore the image.
The camera failure permanently terminated live television broadcasts of the moonwalks almost immediately after they began.
With live TV dead, visual documentation of Conrad and Bean on the surface relied primarily on Hasselblad still cameras and a 16mm movie camera.
Conrad and Bean conducted two moonwalks, during which they detached and retrieved parts of the Surveyor 3 probe to bring back to Earth.
Pete Conrad's first words upon stepping onto the lunar surface were chosen to win a bet with a reporter over whether astronaut remarks were scripted.
Following the Apollo 12 mishap, NASA implemented procedural safeguards including mandatory lens caps when relocating surface cameras.
Starting with Apollo 15, control of lunar surface color TV cameras was shifted to Mission Control operators rather than astronauts.
Later in life, Alan Bean became a professional artist who spent decades painting scenes of his lunar experiences.
The ALSEP scientific experiment packages left behind by Apollo crews operated on the Moon until NASA deactivated them on September 30, 1977 due to budget constraints.

disputed: Whether the camera burn was caused by direct sunlight or high-intensity reflection off the lunar module: early on Bean suspected glare from the lander, but post-mission TV analysis confirmed the lens was pointed directly into the Sun while being carried to the tripod. Scripts should specify Bean pointed the camera toward the Sun.
